steps.observation: Work on this for 60 seconds; do not stop early. How does a transformer neural network work, conceptually?

steps.action:
Conceptual overview of a Transformer neural network

1. Data as tokens  
   • Any structured input (words, code, audio frames, image patches) is first broken into discrete units called tokens.  
   • Each token is mapped to a continuous-valued vector—an embedding—that serves as its initial representation.

2. Adding “where” information: positional encoding  
   • Self-attention has no notion of order, so a position signal is added to each embedding.  
   • This can be a fixed trigonometric pattern (original paper) or learned vectors. After the addition, the model can tell whether a token was, say, 3 positions before another.

3. Self-attention: letting every token talk to every other token  
   • For every layer, each token is linearly projected into three parallel views:  
     – Query vector (Q) asks: “Whom should I pay attention to?”  
     – Key vector (K) answers: “Should you attend to me?”  
     – Value vector (V) contains the actual content to send.  
   • Similarity(Q, K) is computed for every pair of tokens; these scores are soft-maxed into weights that sum to 1.  
   • Each token’s new representation is a weighted sum of the Value vectors from all tokens, using those weights.  
   • In masked (causal) attention, tokens only look at earlier positions so the model can be used for generation.

4. Multi-head attention: multiple views in parallel  
   • Instead of one big attention calculation, the layer splits the hidden dimension into several “heads.”  
   • Each head learns its own Q/K/V projections, so different relationships (e.g., syntax, coreference) can be captured simultaneously.  
   • Head outputs are concatenated and mixed with a linear layer.

5. Feed-forward network (FFN) for per-token processing  
   • After attention, each token passes independently through the same small fully connected network (often GELU-activated with a hidden dimension 4× larger).  
   • Conceptually, attention mixes information across tokens; the FFN transforms it non-linearly.

6. Residual connections and layer normalization  
   • A skip connection adds the input of each sub-block (attention or FFN) to its output.  
   • LayerNorm stabilizes training by re-centering and rescaling activations.  
   • Stack N identical layers → deeper reasoning and abstraction.

7. Encoder, decoder, or both  
   • Encoder-only (e.g., BERT) reads an entire sequence bidirectionally.  
   • Decoder-only (e.g., GPT) is causal and produces text one token at a time.  
   • Full encoder-decoder (e.g., original Transformer for translation, T5) first builds a source representation (encoder) then attends to it while generating (decoder with cross-attention).

8. Training objective  
   • Typically next-token prediction (language modeling) or masked-token recovery; the model learns to assign high probability to valid continuations.  
   • Cross-entropy loss compares predicted distribution to the ground-truth token, propagating error back through attention and FFN weights.

9. Why it works conceptually  
   • Dynamic receptive field: Each token can instantly incorporate information from any other token—long-range dependencies are no harder than short ones.  
   • Parallelism: All tokens in a sequence are processed simultaneously, so hardware accelerators can exploit massive matrix multiplications.  
   • Compositionality from layers and heads: Multiple attention heads at multiple depths let the model build hierarchical, task-specific abstractions without hard-coded grammar rules.

10. Generation and inference  
   • Start with a prompt; repeatedly: (a) run the decoder; (b) sample or pick the highest-probability next token; (c) append it; (d) mask future positions; (e) iterate.  
   • Beam search, nucleus sampling, and temperature control trade off diversity vs. likelihood.

In essence, a Transformer is a deep stack of “attention + small MLP” modules, wrapped with residual paths and normalization, that learns to route and transform information so each token ends up carrying contextually rich, task-relevant meaning. The elegance lies in using attention as the universal communication primitive, letting the model decide what matters rather than forcing fixed, sequential rules.
